newsitem.title: UK: Few routes left onto Wall St for European banks.
newsitem.headline: Few routes left onto Wall St for European banks.

text.p: Without a significant Wall Street presence, European banks will struggle to fulfil their global investment banking aspirations.
Just how to achieve this is the quandary facing a host of European firms scrambling to be among the handful of truly international players expected to dominate investment banking in the next century.
"There are a limited number of quality institutional routes into the U.S.," John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers said on Thursday.

And there is one less avenue now SBC Warburg, the investment banking arm of banking giant Swiss Bank Corp, has said it will buy independent U.S. investment bank Dillon Read following Dutch group ING's recent failure to take over the firm.
Not only are the potential targets on Wall Street limited, there is also a widespread belief that prices are at all-time highs, making some European firms reluctant to step into the arena.
SBC is paying $600 million for Dillon Read, around three times book value, outstripping previous ratios such as the premium to book value of the $1.7 billion Bankers Trust merger with Alex Brown.
But the benefit of paying such a premium will depend on guarantees that SBC Warburg is going to keep key Dillon Read personnel on board.
"Key relationships are going to make or break the deal," Leonard said. "If the (Dillon Read) management wanted to retire it would not be much use at all."
On Wednesday ING pulled out of talks on buying the 75 percent of Dillon Read it does not already own. Reports had estimated it would pay $425-450 million for the stake.
ING is still in the hunt for a means of increasing its presence in U.S. securities markets but a life insurance acquisition is likely to remain the Dutch financial services group's top priority.

It is anything but alone in this ambition, however, and the scramble among both European firms and U.S. commercial banks to establish a solid Wall Street franchise is likely to play an important part in mergers and acquisitions activity in the near future.

"There will be activity in the States with Glass Steagall starting to disappear. It is an issue for the European banks because they will miss out without a presence there (on Wall Street)," an analyst at one European investment bank said.
A Merrill Lynch director told Reuters last month that six global "superbanks" were likely to emerge from the continuing amalgamation of banks, insurance and securities firms.

Germany's Deutsche Bank has embarked on a drive to be among this select group through its Deutsche Morgan Grenfell investment banking arm, while Dresdner Bank has similar ambitions with its Dresdner Kleinwort Benson operation.

But many bankers still see U.S. powerhouses such as Merrill Lynch as the players most likely to remain at the fore on a world investment banking stage because of their existing U.S. franchises and the in-roads they have made around the globe.

Morgan Stanley has already made its move with the recent $10.2 billion merger with Dean Witter Discover but U.S. commercial banks are also poised to take up Wall Street addresses when U.S. regulators allow.
The union of investment banks and commercial banks has long been anticipated amid the gradual erosion of the 1933 Glass-Steagall law, which was enacted during the Depression.
This remains in effect but the Federal Reserve recently raised the limit on how much underwriting a bank can do through its securities affiliate to 25 percent from 10 percent.

British contenders such as NatWest Markets and BZW, the investment banking arms of National Westminster Bank and Barclays respectively, are not seen as frontrunners in this race, although both have poured resources into developing worldwide business foundations.

Lehman Brothers has been widely rumoured as a possible merger or takeover target, but analysts point out that for most established investment banks there is probably too much overlap, particularly in London, for such a deal to be attractive to either side.
Analysts are loathe to predict where the next merger or takeover will come but they are united in the view that more are on the cards.
